questions.question: What does it mean for two metrics $d_p$ and $d_q$ on $\boldsymbol X$ to be topologically equivalent?
options: They give exactly the same distance between every pair of points.
They produce the same collection of open subsets of $\boldsymbol X$.
They are both discrete metrics.
They make every subset of $\boldsymbol X$ finite.

questions.question: What does topological equivalence of two metrics require?
options: They assign exactly the same distance to every pair.
They have the same formula.
They generate exactly the same open subsets.
They make every set finite.

questions.question: If $d_p\sim d_q$ and $\boldsymbol E\subseteq\boldsymbol X$ is open with respect to $d_p$, what follows?
options: $\boldsymbol E$ is closed but not open with respect to $d_q$.
$\boldsymbol E$ is open with respect to $d_q$.
$\boldsymbol E$ must be empty.
$\boldsymbol E$ must equal $\boldsymbol X$.

questions.question: Which pair of metrics is topologically equivalent but not strongly equivalent?
options: The discrete metric is topologically equivalent to every $p$-metric.
Strongly equivalent metrics are never topologically equivalent.
Topologically equivalent metrics must have equal distance values.
$d_{\tan}(x,y)=|\tan x-\tan y|$ is topologically equivalent to $|\cdot|$, not strongly.

questions.question: Which implication between strong and topological equivalence of metrics is valid?
options: Topological equivalence always implies strong equivalence.
Topological equivalence implies the metrics are identical functions.
No two distinct metrics can be topologically equivalent.
Strong equivalence of metrics implies topological equivalence.

questions.question: Which statement captures the interpretation of topologically equivalent metrics?
options: They may measure distances differently but agree on which sets are open.
They must assign the same numerical distance to every pair of points.
They cannot be defined on the same space.
They make open sets unnecessary.

questions.question: Suppose every subset of $\boldsymbol X$ is open under $d_p$, but not every subset is open under $d_q$. What can be concluded?
options: $d_p$ and $d_q$ are strongly equivalent.
$d_p = d_q$ as metrics.
$d_p$ and $d_q$ are not topologically equivalent.
$d_q$ has no open sets.

questions.question: If two metrics are strongly equivalent on $\boldsymbol X$, what can you safely say?
options: They are not topologically equivalent.
They are topologically equivalent.
They define no topology on $\boldsymbol X$.
They must both be the absolute value metric.

questions.question: A student claims: 'Topologically equivalent metrics must be strongly equivalent.' Which example warns against this?
options: The zero vector subspace example.
$d_{\tan}$ versus the absolute value metric.
The Maclaurin series of $\mathrm e^x$
The taxicab norm unit ball

questions.question: Which condition captures topological equivalence of two metrics?
options: A point $x\in\boldsymbol X$ is equal to $y$ precisely when $d_p(x,y) = d_q(x,y)$.
A subset is finite under $d_p$ precisely when it is infinite under $d_q$.
A subset $\boldsymbol E\subseteq\boldsymbol X$ is open with respect to $d_p$ precisely when it is open with respect to $d_q$.
Every ball for $d_p$ has the same radius as every ball for $d_q$.

questions.question: Two metrics on $\boldsymbol X$ produce the same open subsets, but $d_p(x,y)\ \neq d_q(x,y)$ for some points. Which conclusion is consistent with the definition?
options: They cannot be topologically equivalent.
They cannot be metrics.
One of the metrics must be discrete.
They can still be topologically equivalent.

questions.question: What does the discrete-metric example show about topological equivalence with the usual $p$-metrics on $\mathbb{R}^n$?
options: The discrete metric is not topologically equivalent to the usual $p$-metrics.
The discrete metric is strongly equivalent to every $p$-metric.
Every $p$-metric gives the discrete topology.
The discrete metric cannot define open sets.

questions.question: When are two metrics topologically equivalent?
options: They give exactly the same numerical distances.
They determine the same open subsets of the space.
They are both equal to the discrete metric.
They make every set finite.

questions.question: Which notation denotes topological equivalence of $d_p$ and $d_q$?
options: $d_p\sim d_q$
$d_p\approx d_q$ only
$d_p\subset d_q$
$d_p\cup d_q$

questions.question: What do topologically equivalent metrics agree on?
options: The exact distance between every pair
Which subsets are open
The value of every sequence term
The dimension of the space only

questions.question: If a set $E$ is open under $d_p$ and $d_p\sim d_q$, what follows?
options: $E$ is closed but not open under $d_q$.
$E$ is empty.
$d_p=d_q$ pointwise.
$E$ is open under $d_q$.

questions.question: If two metrics are strongly equivalent, what topological conclusion follows?
options: They cannot have the same topology.
They must be identical functions.
They are not metrics.
They are topologically equivalent.

questions.question: Which example is topologically equivalent to the absolute value metric but not strongly equivalent?
options: The discrete metric and a $p$-metric
$d_{\tan}(x,y)=|\tan x-\tan y|$
The zero function
Any non-metric distance

questions.question: Why can topologically equivalent metrics measure distances differently?
options: It requires all distances to be equal.
Same open sets, not necessarily same distances.
It ignores open sets completely.
It applies only to finite spaces.

questions.question: If a sequence convergence statement is based only on open sets and two metrics are topologically equivalent, which expectation is natural?
options: It should be unchanged under replacing one metric by the other.
The statement must reverse direction.
The sequence must become finite.
The two metrics must be strongly equivalent first.
